analysis.one_liner: Restores government power to regulate cable TV subscription rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: introduced with zero cosponsors, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed a 1996 law that bans the FCC and local franchise authorities from regulating cable television rates, and restored the rate-regulation rules that existed under the Communications Act of 1934. In plain terms, it would have let government regulators cap what cable companies could charge subscribers. It never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, whose monthly bills would have been subject to regulation by the FCC and local franchising authorities if the bill had passed.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 that prohibits the FCC and local cable franchising authorities from regulating cable television service rates, reinstating the authority they had under the Communications Act of 1934.
Takes effect 90 days after enactment, so rate regulation would have resumed quickly.

analysis.who_pays: Cable television operators, who would lose pricing freedom and face FCC and local regulation of the rates they charge subscribers.

drawbacks.text: Reimposing rate regulation could reduce cable companies' incentives to invest in network upgrades and new services, a standard concern about price controls in capital-intensive industries.

The 1996 deregulation was adopted on the theory that competition would emerge and hold prices down; the bill would reverse that policy choice rather than replace it with an alternative approach, and the record provided does not include evidence on whether competition had or had not materialized.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subscribers facing rising cable bills, restored rate regulation offered a direct price benefit. The trade-off is the standard one for price controls: lower bills in the short run, with a possible cost in slower network investment. The bill was a one-page reversal of the 1996 deregulation with no findings or alternative safeguards, so its design was blunt, and it never advanced far enough to be refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to its telecommunications subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barney Frank introduced the Cable Consumer Rights Act of 2005 on April 20, 2005.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On May 13, 2005, it was referred to the subcommittee on telecommunications and the internet, and the public record shows no further action.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable television operators, which kept their freedom from federal and local rate regulation. Subscribers gained nothing, as no version of the bill ever reached a vote.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore FCC and local authority over cable rates.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its telecommunications subcommittee and took no further action, so the bill never received a hearing or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded support or opposition beyond the single Democratic sponsor; no cosponsors signed on and no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the 1996 prohibition on cable rate regulation, exposing operators' subscription pricing to FCC and local franchise authority caps. Its defeat left their pricing unregulated, which is what subscribers pay for cable service.

industries.industry: Telecommunications and internet subcommittee jurisdiction holders (telephone and media companies with stakes in cable policy)
industries.note: The 1996 deregulatory framework that the bill would have unwound remained untouched, keeping the communications industry's rate-setting freedom intact. The bill posed no threat to it because it never left committee.
